title: Was There A Real Robin Hood?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore whether a real Robin Hood existed. They cover the medieval setting (often placed in the Tudor era by mistake) and historians who place a real figure around the early thirteenth century. They discuss the earliest ballads (Piers Plowman, 1377, and the Middle English Robin Hood ballads), the royal forest and forest laws that made forest-dwellers outlaws, and King Richard the Lionheart and King John, including Richard's death and John's reign and the Magna Carta. They examine candidates such as Robin Hood as a generic term for outlaw (the 1262 Robohad record), Fulk fitz Warin, Eustace the Monk, and Roger Godbeard (Brian Benison's claim), and touch on Maid Marian, the 2018 Robin Hood film, and Robin Hood's supposed death at the hands of a prioress. The episode ends with listener mail about roundabouts.
topics: was there a real Robin Hood

segments.title: Opening banter and Robin Hood movie references
segments.summary: Hosts banter about a paper clip holding Josh's glasses and a quote from the movie Role Models, then introduce Robin Hood as the topic, noting the legend is usually set in the wrong era.

segments.title: Was there a real Robin Hood and the ballads
segments.summary: Historians disagree on whether a real Robin Hood existed, with some placing him in the early thirteenth century. The hosts discuss how early historians filled gaps with invented material. They cover the earliest ballads, including Piers Plowman (about 1377) and the Middle English Robin Hood ballads, and how oral tradition could preserve history.

segments.title: Medieval forests and forest laws
segments.summary: Forests covered a large share of England and were royal hunting land. Forest laws made living there illegal, so forest-dwellers became outlaws and fought the King's officials, which explains why the forest is the setting of the legends.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break for the show's sponsor read.

segments.title: King John, Richard the Lionheart, and the Ballad king
segments.summary: The only king named in the early ballads is Edward, likely Edward III. Popular legend ties Robin Hood to Richard the Lionheart and the villain King John. The hosts describe Richard's death from a crossbow wound and the execution of Peter Basil. They describe John's reign, his taxes, and the Magna Carta, and argue that his rule turned the outlaw into a hero.

segments.title: Robin Hood as a generic outlaw term and the 1262 record
segments.summary: Some historians argue that Robin Hood was a generic term for an outlaw rather than a person's name. They cite an 1262 record that describes a man as a robehod, which suggests the term was widely understood by then.

segments.title: Fulk fitz Warin as a Robin Hood candidate
segments.summary: Fulk fitz Warin, a dispossessed nobleman who fought King John from the forest for about three years, is a candidate for the real Robin Hood. The hosts cover his childhood feud with John, his land loss, and his habit of disguising himself and sparing truthful travelers. They also cover Eustace the Monk and the 'fitz' name prefix.

segments.title: Other candidate outlaws and Brian Benison's Roger Godbeard theory
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Pierce of Bretteville, whose men were beheaded by a rival outlaw. They then cover Brian Benison's 2004 book, which argues that Roger Godbeard, a friend of the Sheriff of Nottingham named Reginald Degray, was the real Robin Hood.

segments.title: Early ballad Robin Hood, Maid Marian, and later legends
segments.summary: Early ballads show a more violent Robin Hood who fought local church officials and the Sheriff of Nottingham rather than the king. The hosts note that the altruistic rob-the-rich image came from later Scottish historians, that Maid Marian was added later, and that the Robin Hood story ends with a prioress who over-bled him. They also mention modern film versions.

segments.title: Roundabouts listener mail
segments.summary: A listener from Alexandria, Louisiana writes about a local two-lane roundabout that has frequent crashes and may be replaced. The hosts thank listeners who wrote in about roundabouts and sign off.
